senses.gloss: Very cute and easy to love, especially a child or small animal.
examples: Look at that *adorable* puppy!
Your little boy is absolutely *adorable*.
That was the *most adorable* wedding I've ever been to.

senses.gloss: Showing great love or admiration for someone.
examples: The singer waved to thousands of *adoring* fans.
She gave her husband an *adoring* look.
The grandparents couldn't have been more *adoring*.

senses.gloss: Skillful and quick, especially in handling people or difficult situations.
examples: She's an *adroit* negotiator.
He was *adroit* at avoiding hard questions.
No one in the White House was *more adroit* with the press.

comparison: not gradable — except sense 3, informally *very adult*
contrast: Both stresses are standard in American English: uh-DULT and AD-ult. *An adult* is the noun. *Adult* before a noun often means *sexually explicit* (*adult movies*, *adult content*), so for *for grown-ups* say *for adults* or *grown-up*.

senses.gloss: Fully grown or of legal age.
examples: They have two *adult* children who live out of state.
An *adult* ticket costs twenty dollars.
Most of his *adult* life was spent in Chicago.

senses.gloss: Intended for adults only, usually because it shows sex.
examples: The hotel blocks *adult* channels.
The site has a warning about *adult* content.

senses.gloss: Mature and sensible, as a grown-up should be.
examples: That was a very *adult* way to handle the argument.
Let's try to be *adult* about this.

contrast: Nothing to do with *adult* or *adultery* in meaning. The opposite *unadulterated* is more common, often figuratively: *pure, unadulterated joy*.

senses.gloss: Made weaker or less pure by adding something of lower quality.
examples: The honey turned out to be *adulterated* with corn syrup.
Police seized a shipment of *adulterated* drugs.
The FDA can recall food it finds *adulterated*.

senses.gloss: Involving sex between a married person and someone who is not their husband or wife.
examples: The senator's *adulterous* affair ended his career.
She left her *adulterous* husband.
The relationship was *adulterous* from the start.

contrast: *Advance* means *beforehand*: *advance notice*, *advance tickets*. *Advanced* means *at a high level* or *far along*: *an advanced course*. ✗ *advanced booking* → *advance booking*. *In advance* is an adverb phrase, and *advance* is also a noun and a verb.

senses.gloss: Done, given or happening before an event.
examples: We need at least two weeks' *advance* notice.
*Advance* tickets are cheaper than tickets at the door.
The storm came with very little *advance* warning.

senses.gloss: Going ahead of the main group to prepare.
examples: The president's *advance* team arrived a week early.
An *advance* party checked the campsite.

contrast: Do not confuse with *advance* (beforehand): *advance payment*, not *advanced payment*. For a learner level Americans say *advanced*, not *progressive*.

senses.gloss: Modern and highly developed.
examples: The hospital uses the *most advanced* equipment in the state.
Their technology is far *more advanced* than ours.
It's one of the world's most *advanced* economies.

senses.gloss: At a high level of study or skill.
examples: She's taking *advanced* calculus this semester.
This class is for *advanced* students only.
His English is quite *advanced*.

senses.gloss: Far along in development or time.
examples: The cancer was already at an *advanced* stage.
She's still painting at an *advanced* age.

contrast: The stress moves: AD-van-tij, but ad-vuhn-TAY-juhs.

senses.gloss: Giving an advantage; helpful or favorable.
examples: The deal is *advantageous* to both companies.
It would be *advantageous* for you to speak Spanish.
Buying in the spring is *more advantageous* than waiting until summer.

contrast: Mostly American. It means the same as *adventurous*, which is far more common.

senses.gloss: Willing to take risks and try new things.
examples: *Adventuresome* travelers can hike to the top.
The menu is for *adventuresome* eaters.
She's *more adventuresome* than her brother.

senses.gloss: Willing to try new or risky things.
examples: I'm not very *adventurous* when it comes to food.
Kids get *more adventurous* as they get older.
The architect has a bold, *adventurous* style.

senses.gloss: Full of excitement, new experiences and some danger.
examples: They planned an *adventurous* trip through the Andes.
His early life was pretty *adventurous*.

position: attributive only — almost always before a noun
contrast: *Adverse* describes things (*adverse effects*, *adverse weather*). *Averse* describes a person who dislikes something: *I'm not averse to hard work*. Many Americans also say AD-vurs.

senses.gloss: Harmful or unfavorable.
examples: The drug has few *adverse* side effects.
Flights were canceled because of *adverse* weather.
The *most adverse* conditions were in the mountains.

contrast: *An advisory* is also an American noun for an official warning: *a winter storm advisory*, *a travel advisory*.

senses.gloss: Giving advice but without the power to make decisions.
examples: She sits on the company's *advisory* board.
The committee's role is purely *advisory*.
He was hired in an *advisory* capacity.

contrast: In British English *an aerial* is a TV or radio antenna; Americans say *antenna*.

senses.gloss: Seen or taken from an aircraft or from high above.
examples: The *aerial* photos show how much of the town flooded.
The drone gives you an *aerial* view of the whole farm.
*Aerial* surveys found the missing hikers.

senses.gloss: Happening in the air.
examples: The circus ended with an *aerial* act.
The army began an *aerial* attack at dawn.

contrast: The exercise class is *aerobics*, a noun: *I do aerobics*. The adjective has no *-s*: *aerobic exercise*.

senses.gloss: Of exercise that makes the heart and lungs work harder for a long time.
examples: Swimming is great *aerobic* exercise.
Try to get thirty minutes of *aerobic* activity a day.
Walking fast is *aerobic* if you keep it up.

senses.gloss: Of living things or processes that need oxygen.
examples: *Aerobic* bacteria break down the waste.
The process is *aerobic*, so the tank needs air.

senses.gloss: Shaped so that it moves easily through the air.
examples: The new model is *more aerodynamic*, so it uses less gas.
Cyclists wear *aerodynamic* helmets in races.
The car's shape is very *aerodynamic*.

senses.gloss: Relating to how air moves around objects.
examples: Engineers ran *aerodynamic* tests on the wing.
*Aerodynamic* drag slows the car down at high speed.

senses.gloss: Relating to the science of building and flying aircraft.
examples: He has a degree in *aeronautical* engineering.
The museum has a large *aeronautical* collection.
Pilots have to read *aeronautical* charts.

senses.gloss: Turned into very fine drops or particles that float in the air.
examples: The virus can spread through *aerosolized* droplets.
Some medicines are given in *aerosolized* form.
Once the chemical is *aerosolized*, it's hard to contain.

contrast: Also spelled *esthetic* in American English, especially in medicine and beauty (*esthetician*). *Aesthetic* is also a noun for a style: *the minimalist aesthetic*.

senses.gloss: Relating to beauty, art and how things look.
examples: The building has little *aesthetic* value.
We chose the tiles for *aesthetic* reasons.
It was a practical choice, not an *aesthetic* one.

senses.gloss: Pleasing to look at.
examples: The café is very *aesthetic*, so it's popular on Instagram.
She rearranged the shelves to make them look *more aesthetic*.

senses.gloss: Friendly, relaxed and easy to talk to.
examples: Our new neighbor is an *affable* retired teacher.
He seemed *affable* enough on the phone.
She's the *most affable* person in the office.

position: both — sense 1 also after the noun: *the areas affected*
comparison: not gradable — except sense 2: *more affected*, *most affected*
contrast: *Affected* (influenced) comes from the verb *affect*; *effect* is the noun. The two senses differ: *the affected people* were harmed by something, but *an affected person* behaves in a fake way.

senses.gloss: Influenced or harmed by something.
examples: Aid is being sent to the *affected* areas.
The *most affected* families lost their homes.
Everyone *affected* by the layoffs will get severance.

senses.gloss: Not natural; done to impress people.
examples: She spoke with an *affected* British accent.
His politeness seemed a little *affected*.

senses.gloss: Showing love and warm feelings.
examples: Our cat is very *affectionate* with kids.
He gave her an *affectionate* hug.
My second dog is *more affectionate* than the first.

senses.gloss: Officially connected to a larger group or organization.
examples: The clinic is *affiliated* with the university hospital.
Local *affiliated* stations will carry the game.
He isn't *affiliated* with any political party.

contrast: *Affirmative action* is the American term for policies that favor groups that faced discrimination. *In the affirmative* (formal: *she answered in the affirmative*) uses the noun. On radio, *Affirmative* alone means *yes*.

senses.gloss: Meaning or saying yes.
examples: We need an *affirmative* answer by Friday.
The vote was *affirmative*.
He gave an *affirmative* nod.

senses.gloss: In grammar, stating that something is true rather than asking or denying.
examples: Change the *affirmative* sentences into questions.
In *affirmative* sentences we use *some*, not *any*.

senses.gloss: Suffering from an illness or a serious problem.
examples: He was *afflicted* with arthritis in his later years.
Aid went to the drought-*afflicted* regions.
The city is *afflicted* by high crime.

contrast: Stress the first syllable: AF-loo-uhnt, not uh-FLOO-uhnt.

senses.gloss: Having a lot of money; wealthy.
examples: They live in an *affluent* suburb of Boston.
The area has become *more affluent* in the last decade.
Her family was *affluent* but not famous.

contrast: *Affordable* is about price only. For *easy to reach or use* say *accessible* or *available*.

senses.gloss: Cheap enough that ordinary people can pay for it.
examples: The city needs more *affordable* housing.
Used cars are *more affordable* than new ones.
Is health insurance *affordable* where you live?

contrast: *An Afghan* is also a person from Afghanistan. With a small *a*, *an afghan* is a knitted or crocheted blanket. *Afghani* is the country's currency; using it for the people is common but considered incorrect by many.

senses.gloss: From or relating to Afghanistan.
examples: We ate at an *Afghan* restaurant downtown.
*Afghan* refugees settled in Northern California.
Her father is *Afghan*.

senses.gloss: Being planned or happening, often secretly.
examples: Everyone could tell that something was *afoot*.
Plans are *afoot* to build a new stadium.
There's change *afoot* at the company.

contrast: Formal and legal; in conversation it sounds jokey. *The aforementioned* can also stand alone as a noun.

senses.gloss: Mentioned earlier in the same text or talk.
examples: The *aforementioned* contract expires in June.
Please send the *aforementioned* documents to our office.
My *aforementioned* brother, the one who can't cook, made dinner.

contrast: Most American style guides now drop the hyphen: *African American history*. *Black* (often capitalized) is equally common. It is also a noun: *an African American*.

senses.gloss: Relating to Black Americans whose ancestors came from Africa.
examples: February is *African-American* History Month.
The museum is devoted to *African-American* art.
Her father's side of the family is *African-American*.

contrast: After a verb it is an adverb phrase with no hyphen: *We worked after hours*.

senses.gloss: Happening or open after the usual closing or working time.
examples: They went to an *after-hours* club.
Call the *after-hours* number if it's an emergency.
*After-hours* trading can move the stock price.

contrast: After a verb, no hyphen: *She stays after school*.

senses.gloss: Happening after the school day ends.
examples: Our kids go to an *after-school* program until five.
She has *after-school* soccer on Tuesdays.
The library offers free *after-school* tutoring.

senses.gloss: Having existed for a very long time.
examples: It's the *age-old* question: what came first, the chicken or the egg?
They still make cheese using *age-old* methods.
The festival is an *age-old* tradition.

senses.gloss: Caused by or connected with getting older.
examples: *Age-related* hearing loss is very common.
The doctor said the pain is probably *age-related*.
The study looked at *age-related* changes in the brain.

position: both — sense 1 follows the noun: *children aged 5 to 12*
contrast: Two pronunciations. AYJD in *aged ten* and *aged cheese*; AY-jid in *my aged parents* and *the aged*. Americans often say *age* instead of *aged* with numbers: *children ages 5 to 12*.

senses.gloss: Of a particular age (pronounced AYJD).
examples: The camp is for children *aged* eight to fourteen.
A man *aged* forty was arrested.
Women *aged* 50 and over should get regular checkups.

senses.gloss: Very old (pronounced AY-jid).
examples: She moved home to care for her *aged* parents.
The house was full of *aged* furniture.

senses.gloss: Of food or drink, kept for a long time to improve the flavor (pronounced AYJD).
examples: The steakhouse serves dry-*aged* beef.
Try this *aged* cheddar.

senses.gloss: Never seeming to grow old or go out of date.
examples: At seventy, the actress still looks *ageless*.
The story has an *ageless* appeal.
Good design is *ageless*.

position: both — sense 2 before a noun only
contrast: Sense 1 (annoyed) is very common in spoken American English, though some style guides object and keep *aggravate* for *make worse*.

senses.gloss: Annoyed and impatient.
examples: I get so *aggravated* when people cut in line.
She was *aggravated* with the kids for being late.
He got *more aggravated* the longer he waited.

senses.gloss: In law, of a crime made more serious, for example by using a weapon.
examples: He was charged with *aggravated* assault.
*Aggravated* robbery carries a longer sentence.

senses.gloss: Annoying.
examples: The traffic this morning was really *aggravating*.
It's *aggravating* when the Wi-Fi keeps dropping.
The *most aggravating* part was waiting on hold.

senses.gloss: In law, making a crime or situation more serious.
examples: The judge found no *aggravating* circumstances.
Prior convictions count as an *aggravating* factor.

contrast: The adjective and noun end in -guht; the verb *to aggregate* ends in -gayt. *In the aggregate* (formal) means *in total*.

senses.gloss: Formed by adding many amounts together; total.
examples: *Aggregate* demand fell during the recession.
The team won 5-3 on *aggregate* score.
The report shows the *aggregate* data for all fifty states.

position: attributive only — after a verb it is the passive of *aggregate*

senses.gloss: Collected together from many sources into one group or total.
examples: The app shares only *aggregated* data, not personal details.
Researchers studied *aggregated* results from twelve trials.
*Aggregated* reviews give the movie four stars.

contrast: Russian *агрессивный* is almost always negative, but in American business and sports *aggressive* can be praise: *an aggressive plan*, *aggressive defense*. Double *g*, double *s*.

senses.gloss: Angry and likely to attack or argue.
examples: Keep away from that dog; it's *aggressive*.
He gets *aggressive* when he drinks.
Some drivers are *more aggressive* than others.

senses.gloss: Very determined and forceful in trying to succeed.
examples: The company has an *aggressive* growth strategy.
She's an *aggressive* negotiator.
We need a *more aggressive* marketing campaign.

senses.gloss: Of a disease, spreading fast; of treatment, strong and intensive.
examples: She was diagnosed with an *aggressive* form of cancer.
The doctors recommended *aggressive* treatment.

contrast: American AJ-uhl rhymes with *fragile*; British English says AJ-ile. *Agile* with a capital *A* is also a software development method: *Agile teams*.

senses.gloss: Able to move quickly and easily.
examples: Goats are surprisingly *agile* climbers.
Smaller players tend to be *more agile*.
She's still *agile* at eighty.

senses.gloss: Able to think or react quickly.
examples: He has an *agile* mind.
Small companies can be *more agile* than big ones.

contrast: American spelling is *aging*; British is *ageing*. *Anti-aging* uses the noun.

senses.gloss: Becoming old or older.
examples: Japan has a rapidly *aging* population.
She takes care of her *aging* mother.
The city's water pipes are *aging* and need replacing.

contrast: Russian *агитировать* is *campaign*; English *agitated* is about feeling nervous or upset.

senses.gloss: Nervous, upset and unable to keep calm.
examples: The patient became *agitated* and pulled out his IV.
She seemed *agitated* when she called.
The *more agitated* he got, the faster he talked.

contrast: *An agnostic* is also a noun. In tech, *-agnostic* means *works with any*: *platform-agnostic software*.

senses.gloss: Believing that it is impossible to know whether God exists.
examples: He was raised Catholic but is now *agnostic*.
She describes herself as *agnostic*, not atheist.
They wrote an *agnostic* book about faith.

senses.gloss: Not preferring or committed to any one option.
senses.ru: нейтральный, не привязанный к одному варианту
examples: I'm *agnostic* about which tool we use.
The software is device-*agnostic*.

senses.gloss: Very excited and eager to know or see something.
examples: The whole town was *agog* at the news.
Fans were *agog* waiting for the trailer.
The kids watched, *agog*, as the magician appeared.

position: attributive only — *she agonized over it* is the verb

senses.gloss: Showing great pain or worry.
examples: We heard an *agonized* scream from the next room.
He wore an *agonized* expression.
After weeks of *agonized* debate, they sold the house.

contrast: American spelling with *-z-*; British *agonising*.

senses.gloss: Causing great physical or mental pain.
examples: It was an *agonizing* decision.
The wait for test results was *agonizing*.
Losing in the final minute is the *most agonizing* way to lose.

senses.gloss: Having an extreme fear of open or public places.
examples: She became *agoraphobic* and stopped leaving the apartment.
The film is about an *agoraphobic* writer.
Crowds make him feel almost *agoraphobic*.

senses.gloss: Relating to farming and land, especially as a way of life.
examples: Before 1900, the U.S. was largely an *agrarian* society.
The region still has an *agrarian* economy.
Jefferson dreamed of an *agrarian* republic.

contrast: *I agree* is the everyday way to say *я согласен*. *I'm agreeable to that* is formal, and ✗ *I'm agreeable with you* is wrong.

senses.gloss: Pleasant and easy to like.
examples: We spent an *agreeable* evening on the porch.
He's a very *agreeable* person to work with.
The weather was *more agreeable* than we expected.

senses.gloss: Willing to accept or agree to something.
examples: Is Tuesday *agreeable* to everyone?
The landlord seemed *agreeable* to lowering the rent.

contrast: *Agreed!* alone means *I agree*. *We're agreed* means *we all agree*.

senses.gloss: Decided or accepted by everyone involved.
examples: They met at the *agreed* time.
He was paid less than the *agreed* price.
The terms were *agreed* in advance.

senses.gloss: Of people, having the same opinion.
examples: Are we all *agreed* on the plan?
Everyone was *agreed* that we should leave early.

senses.gloss: Relating to farming.
examples: Iowa is a major *agricultural* state.
Most of the land around here is *agricultural*.
*Agricultural* workers were hit hard by the drought.

position: attributive only — *she has been ailing* is the verb

senses.gloss: Sick, especially for a long time.
examples: He flew home to see his *ailing* father.
The *ailing* singer canceled her tour.

senses.gloss: Of a business or economy, in a weak or failing condition.
examples: The new CEO promised to rescue the *ailing* company.
Congress passed a bill to help the *ailing* economy.

senses.gloss: Without a purpose or direction.
examples: After college he drifted through a few *aimless* years.
The conversation felt *aimless*.
The second half of the movie is even *more aimless*.

senses.gloss: Kept cool by an air conditioner.
examples: We waited in an *air-conditioned* lobby.
Is the bus *air-conditioned*?
Most American cars are *air-conditioned*.

ru: в воздухе; переносимый по воздуху; воздушно-десантный

senses.gloss: Flying or in the air.
examples: The plane was *airborne* within seconds.
Once we were *airborne*, the flight attendants served drinks.

senses.gloss: Carried through the air.
examples: The disease is spread by *airborne* particles.
Some pollen is *airborne* for miles.

senses.gloss: Of soldiers, trained to be dropped from aircraft.
examples: He served in the 82nd *Airborne* Division.
*Airborne* troops landed behind enemy lines.

senses.gloss: Feeling sick because of the motion of an aircraft.
examples: I always get *airsick* on small planes.
An *airsick* passenger asked for a bag.
Take this pill if you're prone to feeling *airsick*.

senses.gloss: Closed so tightly that no air can get in or out.
examples: Store the cookies in an *airtight* container.
Make sure the lid is *airtight*.
The seal on the jar wasn't *airtight*.

senses.gloss: Of an argument or excuse, having no weak points.
examples: The suspect had an *airtight* alibi.
Their case against him seemed *airtight*.

senses.gloss: Of an aircraft, safe and fit to fly.
examples: Inspectors declared the plane *airworthy*.
Every *airworthy* jet was put back in service.
The FAA said the old helicopters were no longer *airworthy*.

senses.gloss: Of a room or building, full of light and fresh air, with a lot of space.
examples: The new office is bright and *airy*.
Taking down the wall made the kitchen much *airier*.
It's the *airiest* apartment we've seen.

senses.gloss: Very light and soft.
examples: She baked a light, *airy* sponge cake.
The fabric is thin and *airy*.

senses.gloss: Casual and not serious, as if something doesn't matter.
examples: He dismissed the problem with an *airy* wave of his hand.
Her promises sounded *airy* and vague.

position: predicative only — never before a noun: *a half-open door*

senses.gloss: Of a door or window, slightly open.
examples: The front door was *ajar* when we got home.
Leave the window *ajar* so the cat can get out.
The car beeped because a door was *ajar*.

senses.gloss: Of arms, with hands on the hips and elbows pointing out; of legs, spread wide apart.
examples: She stood in the doorway with arms *akimbo*.
The coach stood, arms *akimbo*, glaring at the team.
The toddler sat on the floor, legs *akimbo*.

position: both — also right after the noun: *pasta al dente*
contrast: Italian for *to the tooth*. Written as two words, no hyphen. After *cook* it works like an adverb: *cook the pasta al dente*.

senses.gloss: Of pasta or vegetables, cooked so that it is still slightly firm when you bite it.
examples: Boil the spaghetti until it's *al dente*.
I like my vegetables *al dente*, not mushy.
She served *al dente* penne with fresh tomatoes.

contrast: Also a noun: *an Alaskan*. *Alaska Native* (not *Alaskan Native*) is the preferred term for the Indigenous peoples.

senses.gloss: From or relating to Alaska.
examples: We took an *Alaskan* cruise last summer.
The *Alaskan* wilderness is huge.
My roommate is *Alaskan*.

contrast: *Albanian* is also the noun for the people and the language: *She speaks Albanian*.

senses.gloss: From or relating to Albania.
examples: There's a big *Albanian* community in the Bronx.
He's *Albanian*, but he grew up in Italy.
We tried traditional *Albanian* food.

contrast: *An alcoholic* is the noun for the person. *Alcoholic drinks* contain alcohol; Americans say *soft drinks* or *nonalcoholic drinks* for the rest.

senses.gloss: Containing alcohol.
examples: No *alcoholic* beverages are allowed in the park.
Is this punch *alcoholic*?
Kombucha can be slightly *alcoholic*.

senses.gloss: Addicted to alcohol, or caused by that addiction.
examples: She grew up with an *alcoholic* father.
He died of *alcoholic* liver disease.

contrast: *Alert* is also a noun (*a weather alert*, *on high alert*) and a verb (*alert the police*). *On the alert* uses the noun.

senses.gloss: Watching carefully and ready to notice danger or problems.
examples: Drivers need to stay *alert* on long trips.
An *alert* neighbor called 911.
Parents should be *alert* to signs of bullying.

senses.gloss: Awake and able to think clearly.
examples: I feel *more alert* after a cup of coffee.
Grandpa is ninety but still very *alert*.

senses.gloss: Relating to or using algebra.
examples: Solve the *algebraic* equation for x.
The textbook explains *algebraic* expressions step by step.
Students learn *algebraic* thinking in middle school.

senses.gloss: From or relating to Algeria.
examples: She's writing a book on *Algerian* history.
His parents are *Algerian*.
The *Algerian* team scored in the last minute.

senses.gloss: Done by or relating to an algorithm, a set of steps a computer follows.
examples: *Algorithmic* trading now makes up most stock trades.
The feed is fully *algorithmic*.
Critics worry about *algorithmic* bias in hiring.

contrast: *An alien* is the noun (a being from another planet, or in U.S. law a foreign citizen). *Alien* is not a neutral word for *чужой* between people: ✗ *an alien man* → *a stranger*.

senses.gloss: Strange and unfamiliar.
examples: Big-city life felt *alien* to her at first.
Lying is completely *alien* to his nature.
Every year the music scene seems *more alien* to me.

senses.gloss: From another planet.
examples: The movie is about an *alien* invasion.
Scientists are searching for *alien* life.

senses.gloss: Of plants and animals, brought from another part of the world.
examples: *Alien* species are pushing out native fish.
The weed is *alien* to North America.

senses.gloss: Feeling that you do not belong or are cut off from others.
examples: Many young voters feel *alienated* from both parties.
He grew *alienated* from his family.
Remote workers can feel *more alienated* than office staff.

senses.gloss: Making people feel unwelcome or cut off.
examples: The jargon is *alienating* to new customers.
Moving to a new country can be an *alienating* experience.
His comments were even *more alienating* than his policies.

contrast: The *g* is silent: uh-LYND.

senses.gloss: Arranged in a straight line or in the right position.
examples: Make sure the pictures are *aligned*.
The wheels aren't properly *aligned*.

senses.gloss: Agreeing with or supporting a person, group or goal.
examples: Our goals are *aligned* with the company's mission.
The group is *more closely aligned* with the Democrats.
Everyone on the team needs to be *aligned*.

senses.gloss: Having a pH above 7; the opposite of acid.
examples: The soil here is too *alkaline* for blueberries.
Buy *alkaline* batteries; they last longer.
Adding lime makes the water *more alkaline*.

type: evaluative — a phrase used as an adjective
contrast: *Alright* is common in informal writing but still marked wrong by many teachers and editors; *all right* is always safe. *It went all right* is an adverb, and *All right, let's go* is an interjection.

senses.gloss: Not hurt, sick or upset; safe.
examples: Are you *all right*? That looked like a bad fall.
Don't worry, the kids are *all right*.
She felt sick this morning, but she's *all right* now.

senses.gloss: Acceptable or good enough, but not great.
examples: The movie was *all right*, I guess.
His cooking is *all right*.

senses.gloss: Allowed or acceptable to someone.
examples: Is it *all right* if I leave early?
Friday is *all right* with me.

type: compound — phrase used as an adjective; also quality
contrast: American *all-around*; British *all-round*. In gymnastics, *the all-around* is also a noun for the combined event.

senses.gloss: Good at many different things.
examples: He's a great *all-around* athlete.
She's a talented *all-around* musician.
We need an *all-around* player, not just a shooter.

senses.gloss: Overall; including everything.
examples: It was an *all-around* great day.
She won the *all-around* title in gymnastics.

senses.gloss: Including or affecting everything.
examples: The new law is *all-encompassing*.
Grief can feel *all-encompassing*.
They wanted an *all-encompassing* plan, not a quick fix.

contrast: Already extreme, so not *very all-important* or *more all-important*. Often used with *the*: *the all-important final exam*.

senses.gloss: Extremely important.
examples: Now for the *all-important* question: who's paying?
The *all-important* Iowa vote is next week.
In this business, timing is *all-important*.

senses.gloss: Including everything, especially everything in one price.
examples: We booked an *all-inclusive* resort in Cancún.
The price is *all-inclusive*: meals, drinks and tips.
This list isn't meant to be *all-inclusive*.

senses.gloss: Knowing everything.
examples: Many religions describe God as *all-knowing*.
The story has an *all-knowing* narrator.
Don't treat the internet as some *all-knowing* oracle.

contrast: After a verb it is an adverb phrase with no hyphen: *We studied all night*. *An all-nighter* is a night spent awake working.

senses.gloss: Lasting all night or open all night.
examples: We found an *all-night* diner off the highway.
The dorm threw an *all-night* party.
The pharmacy on Main Street is *all-night*.

type: compound — phrase used as an adjective
contrast: After a verb, no hyphens: *It's all or nothing*.

senses.gloss: Allowing only complete success or complete failure, with nothing in between.
examples: Don't take an *all-or-nothing* approach to dieting.
It was an *all-or-nothing* bet.
Perfectionists often have *all-or-nothing* thinking.

contrast: The adverb phrase has no hyphen: *They went all out for the party*.

senses.gloss: Using all possible effort or force.
examples: The two countries were close to *all-out* war.
The team made an *all-out* effort in the second half.
It turned into an *all-out* brawl.

senses.gloss: Having complete power.
examples: The king was *all-powerful*.
The movie villain is an *all-powerful* AI.
People once saw the party boss as *all-powerful*.

senses.gloss: Useful for many different jobs.
examples: Use two cups of *all-purpose* flour.
Grab the *all-purpose* cleaner under the sink.
It's a good *all-purpose* knife for camping.

senses.gloss: The highest, lowest or best ever recorded.
senses.ru: рекордный, небывалый, величайший за все время
examples: Gas prices hit an *all-time* high this summer.
It's my *all-time* favorite movie.
He's the NBA's *all-time* leading scorer.

senses.gloss: Made to be used in any kind of weather.
examples: We put *all-weather* tires on the car.
The school built an *all-weather* track.
Buy an *all-weather* jacket for the trip.

position: attributive only — *he is alleged to...* is the passive verb
contrast: One syllable in *-ged*: uh-LEJD, but the adverb *allegedly* is uh-LEJ-id-lee. Reporters use *alleged* because nothing has been proved: *the alleged killer*.

senses.gloss: Said to be true or to have happened, but not yet proved.
examples: The *alleged* thief was arrested at the airport.
She denies the *alleged* abuse.
He's accused of an *alleged* $2 million fraud.

senses.gloss: Using characters and events to represent a hidden moral or political meaning.
examples: *Animal Farm* is an *allegorical* novel about the Soviet Union.
The painting is clearly *allegorical*.
Some readers take the story in an *allegorical* sense.

contrast: Capital *Allied* refers to the countries that fought Germany and Japan in World War II: *the Allied invasion*. Many Americans say uh-LYD after a verb: *closely allied with*.

senses.gloss: Joined with others by a political or military agreement.
examples: *Allied* forces landed in Normandy in 1944.
The two countries are *allied* with the U.S.
NATO and *allied* governments issued a statement.

senses.gloss: Closely related or connected.
examples: She works in nursing and other *allied* health professions.
Bravery is often *allied* with recklessness.

senses.gloss: Using several words that start with the same sound.
examples: *Peter Piper picked* is an *alliterative* phrase.
Brand names like *Coca-Cola* are *alliterative*.
The poem's *alliterative* lines are fun to read aloud.

position: attributive only — *time was allotted* is the passive verb

senses.gloss: Given or set aside for a particular person or purpose.
examples: Please finish the test in the *allotted* time.
Each speaker has an *allotted* ten minutes.
We went over our *allotted* budget.

senses.gloss: Permitted by the rules or the law.
examples: What's the maximum *allowable* weight for a carry-on bag?
Home office expenses are *allowable* deductions.
Is a second attempt *allowable* under the rules?

senses.gloss: Attractive and exciting in a mysterious way.
examples: The idea of working from a beach is *alluring*.
She had an *alluring* smile.
The offer became even *more alluring* when they doubled the salary.

position: attributive only — after the noun in *God Almighty*
contrast: *The almighty dollar* is an American phrase criticizing the power of money. *God Almighty!* is also an exclamation of surprise or anger, which some people find offensive.

senses.gloss: Having unlimited power, especially of God; also used ironically of money.
examples: They prayed to *Almighty* God.
Everything in this town comes down to the *almighty* dollar.
Some fans treat the coach as if he were *almighty*.

senses.gloss: Unfriendly and not wanting to get involved with other people.
examples: The new manager seemed cold and *aloof*.
She kept herself *aloof* from office gossip.
Cats are often *more aloof* than dogs.
